Senses.Explanation: Literally, 'pure regulations': the binding code governing a Chan monastic community. The term occurs 285 times in 81 allowlisted texts. Chan usage particularly associates it with Baizhang: one discourse calls 'Baizhang's monastic code' an enduring model and says that when put into use its commands are sternly arrayed; another encounter pairs Mazu's establishment of the Chan hall with Baizhang's making of the code. The term also functions as an enforceable house rule. A master tells a departing monk, 'You are a precept-keeping person; why do you not observe the monastic code?' A seasonal address calls the ninety-day confinement of the summer residence the community's monastic code, anchoring the word in scheduled communal regulation rather than an abstract purity ideal. The ordinary wording is thus institutionalized as the named, scheduled, and enforced house regulations of Chan communities, repeatedly traced to Baizhang.
Senses.Note: The literal alternate 'pure regulations' is retained, but 'monastic code' states the observable corpus function in English. Generic references to Baizhang's monastic code (百丈清規) belong here when a passage says Baizhang made it, a community observes it, or its commands operate. The code is an enforceable rule family alongside precepts (戒) and regulations (律), not an optional activity.

Occurrences.Kwic: 你是持戒人，為什不守清規？曰：和尚莫以罪罪人好！
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The exchange treats the code as a rule one can fail to observe and answer for.

Occurrences.Kwic: 三月安居九旬禁足稟如來之教旨乃釋子之清規
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A seasonal address names the ninety-day confinement of the summer residence as the monastic community's code.

Senses.Explanation: The phrase also occurs inside titles of written works that contain or publish monastic regulations. Title matter names The Imperially Revised Baizhang Monastic Code (勅修百丈清規), while another work explicitly says, 'It is titled Monastic Code for Contingent Use in Chan Communities' (目曰禪林備用清規) and explains its title as 'prepared but not necessarily used.' A body of enforceable rules and a named book containing such rules are different objects, so explicit title, volume, catalogue, and table-of-contents uses belong here.
Senses.Note: The surrounding title must be translated case by case; the bare headword does not name one fixed book. A monastic-code preface (清規序), monastic-code volume (清規卷), and monastic-code catalogue (清規目錄) are work signals, not further senses.
